title: Bear found on Japanese fishing boat, escapes into the sea
description: Just when you thought it was safe to go back into the water… Long-time readers of news in Japan will undoubtedly know that we have something of a bear problem. Dwindling human populations in rural areas abandoning farms and homes have allowed a growing ursine population an opportunity to roam further in search of food. […]
content:
Just when you thought it was safe to go back into the water…

Long-time readers of news in Japan will undoubtedly know that we have something of a bear problem. Dwindling human populations in rural areas abandoning farms and homes have allowed a growing ursine population an opportunity to roam further in search of food. As a result, people and bears are increasingly coming face to face, often with tragic results.

And yet, with the vast majority of Japan’s population residing in urban areas, most of us feel like it’s not our problem. Even as bold as they’ve been becoming, bears still tend to stick to the mountains, so as long as we stay away from those, we stay away from bears.

It’s a luxury that fishermen also once enjoyed. After all, it’s not like a bear’s going to suddenly appear out on the open sea… right?

Such a scene was only narrowly avoided when a bear was found hiding out on a fishing boat docked on the coast of Shiogama, Miyagi Prefecture. On 19 September, the one-meter-tall bear was initially spotted on the wharf but took shelter in a longline tuna fishing boat nearby when police arrived.

▼ News report on the potential stowaway bear

The boat had three crew members on board who hid inside private cabins while the animal was roaming the decks. Meanwhile, police cordoned off the area and city officials also arrived to help monitor the bear’s movements.

They planned to wait until dawn to order local hunters in to kill the bear, but at around 1 a.m. the bear evaded local law enforcement by jumping from the boat and into the sea. Authorities monitored the nearby shoreline to see where it would surface but were unable to find the animal.

Bears have shown a very strong talent for evading police cordons in the past as well. That, combined with the fact that it only appeared to be innocently roaming around without injuring anyone, made it hard to not feel a little good that the situation was resolved without any human or animal getting hurt. As such, many online comments were quick with jokes about it.

“Looks like it ‘bearly’ got away!”
“Bear has learned the unique skill: Bear Swim.”
“A bear that doesn’t swim is just an ordinary bear.”
“Imagine going to the beach and seeing a bear swim in from the sea.”
“It’s surprising how many people know bears can swim really well.”
“Maybe it just wanted to apply for a job.”
“Shark bear.”
“If that bear managed to sneak aboard while they set sail, it would have been a perfect b-movie plot.”
“Bears are everywhere!”

That last comment is probably the key takeaway from all this. With each passing year, there are fewer and fewer places in Japan where we can safely say, “Well, at least I don’t have to worry about getting attacked by a bear here.”

But it still seems as if very little is being done to address the issue. Japan’s hunters are getting older with each passing year, and few younger people are interested enough to overcome the country’s strict gun laws to take up such work. Hopefully, those in the national government nestled in a relatively bear-free part of Metropolitan Tokyo won’t choose to ignore this particular problem until it swims up and bites them in the ass.

title: Beautiful Studio Ghibli coin/card cases recreate scenes and props from anime classics [Photos]
description: What better place to carry your train pass than inside No Face’s Spirited Away train ride? In Japan, the vast majority of transactions involve either coins or a card. Yen coins go all the way up to 500 yen (US$3.15) in denomination, so it’s inevitable that you’re going to accumulate a handful of change if […]
content:
What better place to carry your train pass than inside No Face’s Spirited Away train ride?

In Japan, the vast majority of transactions involve either coins or a card. Yen coins go all the way up to 500 yen (US$3.15) in denomination, so it’s inevitable that you’re going to accumulate a handful of change if you’re using cash to buy things or pay for meals, and rechargeable train pass cards like Suica can also be used for purchases at shops and restaurants.

So if you’re traveling in Japan, a card or coin case is a handy thing to have, and a Ghibli anime case is a handy thing to have that’s also awesome.

Studio Ghibli specialty shop Donguri Kyowakoku has designed a series of combination coin/card cases featuring artifacts and characters from some of their most beloved animated films. Starting things off is this embroidered trio of No Face, Boh, and Yu-Bird taking a ride on the train seen in Spirited Away.

The reverse side of the case features the film’s name and an understated illustration, and when you open up the zipper, and you’ll find two compartments inside, allowing a layer of organization for different types of coins or cards.

Other charming details include Boh and Yu-Bird taking a nap on the extendable strap’s connecting-piece reel and a caterpillar-shaped zipper pull.

An especially clever design point is that the windows on the train are actually see-through, adding to the illusion that the characters are actually passing by scenery outside their train carriage.

▼ Though Boh and Yu-Bird are kind of in the emperor of Japan’s seat.

Next up we have another Ghibli character depicted in his most memorable setting: Calcifer peeking out from a cast-iron frying pan.

The Howl’s Moving Castle fire spirit is in the middle of cooking up the hearty breakfast seen in the movie, one of the most mouthwatering of all Ghibli meals. Fittingly, the zipper pull for this pouch is shaped like a spoon, while the strap-connecting piece is a recreation of the multicolored dial next to the castle’s front door that allows the dwelling’s entrance to magically connect to different locations.

The Calcifer pouch is the only one we’re looking at today with only a single shared interior section, so we’re back to two compartments for the My Neighbor Totoro case.

Instead of being shaped like the cuddly studio mascot himself, this pouch is modeled after the container of caramels that sisters Mei and Satsuki share some snacks from early in the movie while they ride in the back of the moving truck on their way to their new home in the most idyllic of Ghibli countrysides.

You do get some Totoro embroidery on the front of the pouch, though, and hanging out around back, as well as on the strap connector, are a bunch of Soot Sprites…

…and the zipper pull this time is caramel-shaped.

And finally, while it may not be candy-related, the fourth pouch is also very sweet…

…since it’s modeled on the party invitation that Tombo gives to enterprising witch Kiki in Kiki’s Delivery Service.

As is often the case with Kiki’s merchandise, black cat Jiji is more prominently featured that the titular protagonist herself, though Kiki’s likeness, of a sort, does still appear on the reel and zipper pull.

Though there’s a lot of variety in the designs, they’re all identically priced at 3,190 yen (US$20). Though the Whisper of the Heart book-design pouch seen at the very start of this article is still out of stock, all of the others have recently been restocked and are available through the Donguri Kyowakoku online store here.

title: Japan restarts at-home collection agent visits for public TV fees
description: Japan’s public broadcaster will once again send third-party agents to people’s doors, resuming unpopular tactic of collecting quasi-obligated fees. Imagine you’re sitting at home, and all of a sudden there’s a knock at the door. You go to see who it is, and it turns out to be someone saying that you have to give […]
content:
Japan’s public broadcaster will once again send third-party agents to people’s doors, resuming unpopular tactic of collecting quasi-obligated fees.

Imagine you’re sitting at home, and all of a sudden there’s a knock at the door. You go to see who it is, and it turns out to be someone saying that you have to give them some money, right then and there, to fulfil your civic duty of funding the police or fire department.

That’d be pretty strange. Generally, things that are supposed to be public services are supposed to be funded through tax revenues, not by individual organizations showing up at your home with an outstretched palm. And it would be even weirder if the person asking you for money was not themselves part of the police or fire department, right? And yet, for many years, this was how Japan’s public broadcaster, NHK, did things. NHK would contract with third-party, private-company bill collectors, who would show up at people’s homes, including at night, and ask for money if they didn’t have a record of the occupant having paid their NHK fees recently.

This, as you might imagine, was not a visit that any members of the public enjoyed getting, especially given the aggressive tone and shady tactics some collection agents employed. After years of blowback, in 2023 NHK finally did away with the practice of at-home visits by third-party collection agents, but on Monday, they announced that they’re bringing them back.

NHK fees exist in an unusual legal space. According to Japan’s Broadcasting Act, anyone with a device that is able to receive NHK broadcasts is required to pay an annual fee of 12,276 yen (US$77), and for those with devices capable of receiving not just NHK’s terrestrial broadcasts but their satellite one as well, the free rises to 21,765 yen a year (those who don’t want to cough up a whole year’s worth of fees all at once can opt for a two or six-month plan, but at higher per-month rates).

Note that actually watching the broadcast is not stipulated as being part of the condition for payment. Simply having a TV that receives NHK broadcasts, which TVs sold in Japan do by default, is enough, and NHK holds that since they produce online content as well, now any household where at least one person has a smartphone, tablet, or Internet-connected PC has to pay too.

▼ So score one for anyone who’s still holding out with an old-school cell phone.

Here, though, is where things get messy. That same Broadcast Act that says people have to pay NHK fees? It doesn’t include any sort of punishment for non-compliance. The fact that NHK apparently can’t just receive an equivalent cut from tax revenue, nor is able to send out payment notices that recipients legally have to comply with, casts further doubt on just how legit the system really is. The use of third-party collectors, and also some embezzlement/accounting scandals within NHK, haven’t helped the public broadcaster’s image either, nor inspired confidence that they’re appropriately using the money they do collect.

But NHK is unhappy with the amount of fees it’s been collecting recently, saying that the 585.1 billion yen it gathered in 2025 was down 5 billion yen from the year before. The organization is also concerned that this was the seventh year in a row for fee collection revenue to decline.

▼ Japan’s total population has also been declining for seven years in a row (more than seven, actually), but I’m sure that demographic detail just slipped NHK’s mind.

So NHK will once again be having third-party agents to go to people’s homes and ask them to pay up if they haven’t already. The program has already resumed in parts of Osaka and Hyogo Prefectures, and the current plan is to expand it to large cities like Tokyo and Nagoya first, followed by a potential further spread to smaller-sized communities.

If you’re wondering whether NHK has to pay the collection agents, the answer is yes, and agents get paid higher amounts the more fees they collect. As a matter of fact, NHK has had to reduce the amount they’ll be paying collection agents compared to previous rates, as costs associated with the old arrangement were deemed too high.

NHK is, at least, aware of the bad reputation these tactics have earned them in the past, and is trying to do things a little less abrasively this time around. Instead of sudden, unannounced visits, written notices will be mailed to households first, with in-person visits coming later. It’s not clear whether those who receive a notice will be asked to schedule a visit, or if it’s just a unilateral declaration of when the agent will be coming. The goal, though, is to “achieve understanding and receive payment of fees through polite explanation,” so hopefully no one else is going to get their house tagged for nonpayment.

Source: Sankei Shimbun via Jin, Yomiuri Shimbun, Asahi Shimbun, Japan Times, Bloomberg

title: Converse Japan and one of Japan’s greatest painters combine for fine fowl shoes [Photos]
description: An all-star of the Edo period art world graces a new canvas. The defining detail of Converse’s All Stars series of sneakers is that the shoes are made with canvas. Of course, linguistically, “canvas” can refer not only to sturdy woven fabric, but also a space in which an artist can create, and both of […]
content:
An all-star of the Edo period art world graces a new canvas.

The defining detail of Converse’s All Stars series of sneakers is that the shoes are made with canvas. Of course, linguistically, “canvas” can refer not only to sturdy woven fabric, but also a space in which an artist can create, and both of those meanings apply to Converse Japan’s newest model.

These hi-top kicks are called the All Star IJ HI, and while scholars of classical Japanese painting may be saying “Ah, of course!” as they look at the IJ part of the name, we’ll take a moment to delve into the letters’ significance. Actually, the IJ here is a set of initials, referring to Ito Jakuchu, one of the most celebrated artists of the mid-Edo period.

▼ Ito Jakuchu

Born in 1712, Ito started out life as a grocer who took over his father’s business in Kyoto’s Nishiki Market (the same market that’s now become a major tourist attraction). But what Ito really wanted to do was paint, and what he really wanted to paint was birds…and the birds he really, really wanted to paint were chickens and roosters.

Though they weren’t his only subject matter, Ito found fowl such fine muses that he painted multiple pieces with gunkeizu, or “painting of chickens/roosters” in their title. For the All Star IJ HI, Converse Japan has chosen to adorn the shoes’ canvas with imagery from Ito’s Saboten Gunkeizu, which Ito painted on the sliding doors of Osaka’s Saifukuji Temple in 1789.

▼ Incidentally, while Converse was founded in the U.S. and has been a subsidiary of Nike since 2003, Converse Japan is a separate company, and part of Japan’s Itochu trading company conglomerate.

Having lived his entire life in the Edo period, when Japan was closed off to the rest of the world by decree of the Tokugawa Shogunate, Ito himself would have had little, if any, opportunity to see footwear beyond traditional geta and zori sandals. Nevertheless, his painting makes for a very stylish sneaker motif, mixing bold and colorful imagery without crossing the line into being garish.

The All Star JB HI is priced at 14,300 yen (US$90) and availably exclusively through Japanese shore store ABC Mart, with orders placeable through the chain’s online store here.

title: New Cardcaptor Sakura fashion line delivers magical girl style for real-world ladies
description: Anime-inspired looks with for-fans nods to the classic series. Creative costumes are a hallmark of the magical girl anime genre, and while Japanese fashion brand Axes Femme may not be able to provide you with a sparkly transformation sequence, they are ready to give fans a new line of Cardcaptor Sakura apparel items. These aren’t […]
content:
Anime-inspired looks with for-fans nods to the classic series.

Creative costumes are a hallmark of the magical girl anime genre, and while Japanese fashion brand Axes Femme may not be able to provide you with a sparkly transformation sequence, they are ready to give fans a new line of Cardcaptor Sakura apparel items.

These aren’t full-blown cosplay items that recreate Sakura’s in-anime outfits with 1:1 fidelity, though. Instead, they’re playfully stylish creations that incorporate the visual motifs and iconography of the series in ways that can still be used in non-magical settings too, with separate tops and bottoms that allow you to put together an entire outfit or mix an item in with your preexisting non-Cardcaptor wardrobe.

Starting things off is the Cardcaptor Sakura Cardigan, which comes in not just four colors, but four character themes. Pictured above is the pink Sakura Kinomoto version, and while all four designs feature frog-clasp closures and lacy accents on the sleeves, only Sakura’s has an embroidered crest of cherry blossom petals, feathers, and stars surrounded by rhinestones.

Alternatively, the lavender Tomoyo cardigan’s crest has musical notes and sakura petals. A compass is the crest for the minty green Syaoran design, and the snowflakes found on the back of the Clow and Sakura books represent Yue on the white cardigan.

The same character-inspired color schemes are utilized for Axes Femme’s Cardcaptor Sakura berets, although the Syaroan version is a less minty shade of green.

Aside from the different colors, the designs for the berets are identical, with each featuring embroidered wings, a tassel, and a Kero-chan charm.

Options are a little more limited for the skirts, which have a flowing sequence of embroidered Clow, Sakura, and Clear Cards amidst suns, moons, and cherry blossoms.

The two-tone design, though, means that each of the three designs gives you a double-dose of colors to coordinate with.

If it’s not chilly enough to use a cardigan, there are alternate top options with a pair of blouses.

The high collar features an asymmetrical pattern with the sun on one side and the moon on the other. Also, look closely and you’ll see that the lace trim on the cuffs has little Kero-chans in it!

Speaking of collars, you might have noticed that the photo of the pink cardigan up above features one that’s especially elaborate. This is actually a separate item.

Though the floral/feathery flares are always white, the attachable collar comes in two color schemes for the ribbon and embroidered wings and Sakura Card emblem.

Finally, rounding out the collection is a trio of stoles, combining the card motif of the skirts with the lace trim of the blouses/skirt hems.

Prices range from 4,400 yen (US$28) for the beret to 5,500 yen for the collar and stole, 7,700 yen for the blouse and cardigan, and 9,900 yen for the skirt. The entire lineup is available through the Axes Femme online shop here.

title: Famous Kyoto shrine has a message for foreign tourists who think it’s okay to dance at sacred sites
description: Fushimi Inari Taisha asks visitors to show some respect after dance videos filmed beneath its famous torii gates spark criticism online. One of the things that draws tourists to Kyoto is its shrines and temples, which have been beautifully preserved for centuries. However, as the world changes around these historic sites, new problems have cropped […]
content:
Fushimi Inari Taisha asks visitors to show some respect after dance videos filmed beneath its famous torii gates spark criticism online.

One of the things that draws tourists to Kyoto is its shrines and temples, which have been beautifully preserved for centuries. However, as the world changes around these historic sites, new problems have cropped up, including overtourism and the desire for fame and likes on social media.

As a result, one of Kyoto’s most famous shrines, Fushimi Inari Taisha, has recently become the stage for a number of individuals who think it’s okay to perform dances on its sacred grounds, all in a bid to gain views. After these videos were widely circulated online, they received a fair amount of clapback from viewers who criticised the thoughtless acts, and now the shrine itself has come forward with a message in response to the social media storm.

One of the recent videos, shared on TikTok and Twitter in early September, showed foreign tourists dancing beneath the shrine’s famous torii gates, blocking the path of other visitors who could be seen waiting for the group to finish their routine. Not only were they blocking the path, but members of the group could be seen entering from outside the walkway, interfering with the natural environment, which according to Shinto religion, is considered sacred.

In fact, the entire grounds is considered sacred, including the approach, where a group of Maori women from New Zealand recently filmed themselves while performing a traditional poi dance. This clip was also met with criticism from the wider community, including from New Zealand-born professional wrestler Henare, who is of Maori heritage. He pointed out that dancing in sacred places also goes against Maori customs and apologised for the incident. He said he had tracked down the people involved and asked them to make a substantial donation to Fushimi Inari Taisha as an apology.

▼ The approach is said to be the pathway for the gods, and is so sacred that etiquette dictates visitors should walk on the sides rather than the very middle.

With other dance videos being filmed at the site and shared online, Fushimi Inari Taisha responded on 7 September with a notice in both Japanese and English reminding visitors to observe proper manners. It explained that the shrine grounds are a sacred area and place of prayer with more than 1,300 years of history.

In an interview with Japanese media outlet J-Cast News, the shrine confirmed that videos had indeed been filmed on its grounds and went on to say that staff will approach visitors whenever they spot prohibited or disruptive behaviour.

Although no damage had been reported in connection with the dancing, the shrine said it was disappointed that these visitors failed to understand the cultural significance of the site.

It’s worth remembering that although shrines like Fushimi Inari Taisha are places of beauty, they are not dance studios, and they are not spaces owned by tourists. They are places where spirits reside, gods are worshipped, and people come to pray. And as more people become familiar with temple and shrine etiquette in Japan, the video that you think will go viral might just land you in hot water and leave you being cancelled instead.

title: Studio Ghibli releases new plush mascot character collection with a focus on friendship
description: Unlikely friendships form across anime movie borders with this new range of soft plush toys. One of the big things that makes a Studio Ghibli film so magical is its characters. A lot of the time, though, the most charming characters tend to be the most elusive, hiding out in forests, bathhouses and even a […]
content:
Unlikely friendships form across anime movie borders with this new range of soft plush toys.


One of the big things that makes a Studio Ghibli film so magical is its characters. A lot of the time, though, the most charming characters tend to be the most elusive, hiding out in forests, bathhouses and even a castle in the sky.

Now there’s a way to befriend these characters in real life, and we don’t have to search high and low for them, as they’re being made available in the form of soft plushies at Ghibli’s specialty retail chain Donguri Kyowakoku.

Called “Nakayoshi Mascot“, this collection of cute characters puts the focus on “nakayoshi”, a concept in Japanese that focuses on harmony and getting along well. Under this banner, the plushies are designed to get along with their human owners and each other as well, so that unlikely friendships can be formed across traditional movie borders.

There are 11 characters vying for our attention in the range, starting with the My Neighbor Totoro Nakayoshi Mascots.

▼ Large Totoro (1,980 yen)

The character that we would usually refer to as “Totoro” is actually known as “Large Totoro” in Japan, to help distinguish it from the smaller ones seen in the movie. Despite the name, it stands at around the same height as the smaller Totoros in this collection, at 9 × 9.5 × 9 centimetres (3.5 × 3.7 × 3.5 inches).

▼ All three Nakayoshi Mascot Totoros look as cute from behind as they do from the front, thanks to their plump little tails.

▼ Large Totoro Leaf (2,090 yen)

Because one Totoro just isn’t enough, the collection includes another Large Totoro, this time with a soft leaf, referencing the large leaf that it holds in the film.

▼ Medium Totoro (1,980 yen)

The Medium Totoro brings its blue hues to the range, and is only a tad smaller, at 10 × 8.5 × 8 centimetres.

▼ Small Totoro (1,650 yen)

The Small Totoro, at 8.5 × 5.5 × 8 centimetres  is smaller again, and is particularly adorable with its large eyes and mouthless features imploring us to take it home.

▼ Catbus (2,420 yen)

The grinning Catbus looks even cuter in soft miniature form, and although it towers over the other characters in the movie, here it measures in at 6 × 8.5 × 12.5 centimetres, making it fit in nicely with the other friends in the collection.

▼ Kiki’s Delivery Service – Jiji (2,090 yen)

Moving over to the magical world of Kiki’s Delivery Service, we have the beloved feline from the film representing, with limbs wide open as if it’s waiting for a cuddle.

▼ Kiki’s Delivery Service – Lily (2,090 yen)

Jiji may not have Kiki by his side for this adventure, but girlfriend Lily will gladly keep him company.

▼ Spirited Away – Otori sama (1,980 yen)

The big yellow bath-loving birds from Spirited Away bring their charm to the Nakayoshi range, while Boh Mouse reminds us of the firm friendship that forms between very different characters in the movie.

▼ Spirited Away – Boh Mouse (2,090 yen)

▼ Laputa: Castle in the Sky – Fox Squirrel (2,200 yen)

One of the friendliest furry animals in the world of Ghibli has to be the beautiful fox squirrels from Laputa: Castle in the Sky. Pop this little plushie on your shoulder and you’ll feel like the giant robot, or even Nausicaä from Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind, who also befriends these creatures in her universe.

▼ Princess Mononoke – Kodama (1,650 yen)

Some of the most memorable characters in Princess Mononoke are the bobble-headed kodama that clack away in the forest, exuding an otherworldly, mystical charm. This kodama retains the wide-eyed, off-kilter features that help to maintain its mystique, but is wonderfully soft so you can give it all the friendly cuddles it needs.

This is a very sweet collection of friends that we’re more than happy to welcome into our home, and they can be purchased at Donguri Kyowakoku stores and online (links below). It’ll be tough to choose our favourites, but the temptation to purchase from across the Ghibli worlds to create our own crossover storylines is way too great to resist.

title: Pikachu plushie actually goes into space as part of Pokémon/European Space Agency collaboration
description: Shared spirit of adventure leads to team-up between Pokémon franchise ahead of World Space Week. French astronaut Sophie Adenot is currently on her first trip to space, as part of the European Space Agency’s ongoing Epsilon mission. Adenot isn’t the only one making her maiden voyage beyond Earth’s gravitation pull, though, as she’s been accompanied […]
content:
Shared spirit of adventure leads to team-up between Pokémon franchise ahead of World Space Week.

French astronaut Sophie Adenot is currently on her first trip to space, as part of the European Space Agency’s ongoing Epsilon mission. Adenot isn’t the only one making her maiden voyage beyond Earth’s gravitation pull, though, as she’s been accompanied by another first-time spacefarer: a Pikachu.

Adenot blasted off back in February from Cape Canaveral, but as revealed in a just-released video that was recorded prior to her departure, Adenot took a Pikachu plushie, dressed in an ESA uniform, with her to the International Space Station.

The reveal coincides with the announcement that Pokémon Company is helping promote the ESA’s World Space Week events, which will be taking place from October 4 to 10. The ESA says that the two organizations’ shared values of curiosity and imagination and spirit of adventure are the result of “a common ambition: to inspire new generations to dream big, explore and experiment.”

As part of the celebration, there are two new Pikachu plushies on the way, one male and one female (female Pikachus have a heart-shaped tail tip), as well as crossover pins, patches, tote bags, apparel, and Pokémon Trading Card Game accessories coming to both the Pokémon Center and ESA online stores.

▼ There’s no word as to whether Sailor Moon’s Artemis was part of the ground control team for the Pikachu plushie’s spaceflight.

Though Pokémon is best known for its in-game/anime pseudo-science such as Dragon-type attacks being ineffective against Fairy-type Pokémon or Eevee only being able to evolve into Umbreon under the light of the moon, in recent years the franchise has partnered with a number of educational, scientific, and cultural organizations, as seen in the Pokémon Fossil Museum events, the Pokémon x Crafts Exhibition, and Amsterdam Van Gogh Museum collaboration.

Full details regarding prices and on-sale dates for the Pokémon/ESA crossover merch are yet to be released, but ostensibly they should be available by the start of World Space Week on October 4.

content:
The fantasy of using Cloud’s sword every day can now become a reality.

There’s a whole lot of imagery in anime and video games that looks awesome but would be impractical in the real world. Even within that artistic subgenre, though, Final Fantasy VII’s Buster Sword is an especially extreme example.

Right off the bat, it’s a sword, something that most of us don’t have a use for in our daily lives. Should you somehow happen to have a melee weapon-intensive lifestyle, even then the Buster Sword isn’t a particularly viable choice, since while protagonist Cloud can swing the thing around with ease, it’d be too heavy and bulky to fight with for those of us who have to deal with actual weight and gravity without any assistance from an in-game physics engine.

And yet…the Buster Sword does look really cool, so thankfully Square Enix has come up with a version that can serve a useful purpose for those of us not living in the world of Final Fantasy.

Draped over that dude’s back is the Final Fantasy VII Buster Sword Muffler Towel. Muffler towels (muffler here being used to indicate a scarf, not a part of a car’s exhaust system) are essentially a long face towel, made of material that’s pliable enough to drape over your shoulders or wrap around your neck. A lot of muffler towels bear the names and insignias of sports teams, bands, or idol singers, but this one instead features a print of Cloud’s Buster Sword.

▼ The reverse-side has longer loops to better wick away moisture.

Muffler towels are especially popular at fan events, where dampening them with water before putting one on your shoulders is a great way to counteract the heat generated by large crowds. With a length of 128.5 centimeters (50.6 inches), though, the Buster Sword towel is large enough to make a striking statement as home décor, hung on a wall or next to a sink.

It’s available for preorder through the Square Enix online store here, priced at 1,980 yen (US$12.50) and with a release date of December 19. Just make sure your cat doesn’t get it mixed up with its Buster Sword scratching pad.

title: Denny’s Mapputatsu? Parfait is hiding a big secret in plain sight that splits us down the middle
description: The Mapputatsu? Parfait tackles food waste without sacrificing visuals so that you can still happily feed both yourself and your phone. Back in January, a new style of parfait appeared at Denny’s Japan. From the front it appears as a regular parfait, but from the side, it looks like it’s been split in two–leading to […]
content:
The Mapputatsu? Parfait tackles food waste without sacrificing visuals so that you can still happily feed both yourself and your phone.

Back in January, a new style of parfait appeared at Denny’s Japan. From the front it appears as a regular parfait, but from the side, it looks like it’s been split in two–leading to its name, the Mapputatsu? Parfait (“Two equal parts? Parfait”).

▼ Pictured below are versions with Shine Muscat grapes for 1,078 yen (US$6.87) and with chocolate for 748 yen.

The purpose of this unusual setup is to reduce food waste while still providing a visually attractive, photo-worthy treat for diners. The menu even provides statistics that 54 percent of diners have ordered food for the sake of posting photos on social media and one out of three have left their dessert unfinished at family-style restaurants in Japan. With parfaits typically looking like veritable works of food art but also being on the larger side, we can assume that they’re one of the more common menu items that diners order for the visual spectacle but aren’t able to finish.

Initially, the Mapputatsu? Parfait was only available at two Denny’s Japan locations, but it’s been slowly expanding onto menus across the country. We happened to be in the area of Saitama-Shintoshin’s Cocoon City shopping complex branch recently and decided to swing by to finally try it out.

Once we sat down and peeked at the digital tablet menu, we were excited to see it in all of its question-asking glory. It was a tough choice but we ordered the Shine Muscat version.

It arrived about 10 minutes later. We took a moment to admire its striking visuals from head-on, the way the waiter had placed it down on the table in front of us.

Unsuspecting diners would never know…

…that the reverse side held a big secret: the parfait glass indeed looked like it had been split straight down the middle!

▼ Even the grapes were cleanly sliced in half.

Thankfully, that didn’t mean the glass was in any danger of collapsing, but just that the vessel was only half the width of a regular one.

We had a train to catch soon, so it was time to dig in. It was still blowing our minds that even viewed from the top it looked like a perfectly ordinary parfait.

The Shine Muscat grapes were, as usual, tantalizingly sweet and refreshing. They meshed wonderfully with the layers of sorbet and jelly lining the inside of the glass. It felt good to know that we were still getting everything that we would from a normal parfait.

The sweet treat as a whole was truly the perfect size to feel full in a comfortable–not sickly–way.

Some readers might be asking, “Why not just order a mini parfait instead?” Mini parfaits in smaller glass dishes also exist at Denny’s Japan, so that’s always a possibility. However, we have to admit that there’s something special about the thrill of having a tall parfait placed in front of you that a shorter one just can’t replace.

Please note that not all Denny’s Japan locations may offer the Mapputatsu? Parfait. Those that do may not have all the same versions, either, so it’s best to check ahead of time if there’s a specific flavor that you want. We would strongly recommend the Shine Muscat variety–in fact, it was so good that we’re now hooked on anything with the same taste!

title: Sanrio to release own rhythm game for smartphones next January
description: Hello, tired fingers. Sometimes I wonder if there’s a corner of existence that Hello Kitty and her friends from Sanrio haven’t established a presence in. Electric guitars? Check. Gundam? content:
Hello, tired fingers.

Sometimes I wonder if there’s a corner of existence that Hello Kitty and her friends from Sanrio haven’t established a presence in. Electric guitars? Check. Gundam? Check. Haunted zombie land? Check.

But one place Hello Kitty has yet to appear is a smartphone-exclusive rhythm game (Taiko no Tatsujin doesn’t count because that cameo was on a console version). However, that small patch of reality will soon go without kawaii cats and puppies no longer as Sanrio Kawaii Me Live! is set to be released in January 2027.

In this game, a range of characters from Sanrio’s vast roster, including Hello Kitty, My Melody, Pompompurin, Cinnamoroll, Kuromi, and many more, perform on stage with your help. There are two styles of rhythm play: one involves tapping at the right time when two circles converge in a style somewhat similar to the dance-offs in Final Fantasy VII Remake or Yakuza 0. The other style requires keeping your finger along a horizontal bar and tapping or sliding it on the objects as they fall in a style like Guitar Hero or Beatmania.

The game is free to play, and you’ll get to start off with Sanrio’s own playlist of seven songs based on their characters. There will also be collaboration songs with Polkadot Stingray, Soala, Mi’Line Hearts, Yabai T-Shirts Yasan, Lienel, She’s, and Zutomayo. More songs will also be added over time.

But the real charm in Sanrio Kawaii Me Live! is to do as the title suggests and kawaii up your chosen character. Unlock new outfits and musical equipment for your character to wear and hold, while also designing the stage layout to your personal preference. It seems like any Sanrio fan would want to spend most of their time in this part of the game, but you’ll have to perform to unlock more costumes.

Also, for people in Yokohama, there will be a chance to experience the fun live at a release event on 14 January, 2027 at Yokohama Kannai Hall. There will be live performances by many of the artists mentioned above, and appearances by many of the Sanrio characters mentioned above.

In the meantime, pre-registration for the game is already underway on the App Store and Google Play Store. And to make sure no one dawdles, Sanrio Games is holding a special campaign to unlock in-game items based on how many people pre-register, starting with an energy-boosting Cosmo Soda item at 50,000 people, up to a Hello Kitty dressed in Mira Wear if one million people promise to check out the game.

▼ Mira Wear Hello Kitty

There’s still a way to go before the release of Sanrio Kawaii Me Live! and more details are sure to emerge before then. It seems to me that this title is ripe for Yoshikitty to make an appearance, either as an unlockable character or final boss where you’ll have to wear your fingers out trying to tap through “Kurenai.”

title: US$9,700 solid-gold Pokémon figure going on sale in Japan, life-size gold-leaf Pikachu appears too
description: Artisans create an extremely expensive, and extremely accurate, recreation of a certain Steel/Ghost-type Pokémon. If you’re lucky enough to find an interest in your youth that you can enjoy into your adult years, and also fortunate enough to secure a grown-up job that allows some extra room in your budget for fun stuff, you’ll eventually […]
content:
Artisans create an extremely expensive, and extremely accurate, recreation of a certain Steel/Ghost-type Pokémon.

If you’re lucky enough to find an interest in your youth that you can enjoy into your adult years, and also fortunate enough to secure a grown-up job that allows some extra room in your budget for fun stuff, you’ll eventually find yourself in a situation where you’re pondering splurging on your hobby. Sure, that anime/video game figure is expensive, but it looks cool, and it’ll make you happy, so why not go for it? Live a little!

However, even relatively well-to-do Pokémon fans will probably need some extra time to mull over the series’ latest figure of Gholdengo.

If we were going by looks alone, picking up this figure would be a no-brainer. According to its Pokédex entries, Gholdengo’s body is made of gold, and this figure boasts an appropriately alluring shine. This fidelity to the source material wasn’t achieved with special paint applied to plastic, though, and is instead a result of the figure being made of solid 24-karat gold.

At 6 centimeters (2.4 inches) in height and weighing 15 grams (0.53 ounces), in terms of size and weight the 24-Karat Gholdengo would be perfect for setting on the corner of your desk to mingle with whatever capsule toys or acrylic mini standees reside there. Price-wise, though? This probably deserves a special place where it’s less likely to get knocked off its perch, since the asking price is 1.54 million yen (approximately US$9,700).

That price tag is going to bump the solid-gold Gholdengo out of the reasonable-to-buy range for many fans, but it’s still in the awesome-to-look-at category, and so thankfully the one-of-a-kind piece will be on display at the Takashimaya department store in Yokohama, which is holding the Yokohama Grand Gold Exhibition later this month. Two other golden Pokémon figures will also be on display, a life-size Pikachu (50 centimeters tall) and a life-size Gholdengo (120 centimeters, according to its Pokédex entry).

Instead of being solid gold, the life-size figures are covered in gold leaf, with roughly 200 sheets used for Pikachu and 730 for Gholdengo. Neither one is being offered for sale at the event.

The exhibition will also feature many non-Pokémon pieces, with over 1,000 gold items being shown by participating artisans, such as golden orin singing bowls and figurines of the upcoming Chinese Zodiac animal, the sheep.

The Yokohama Grand Gold Exhibition takes place from September 30 to October 5 in the special event area on the 8th floor of the Yokohama Takashimaya, located right outside Yokohama Station. Admission is free, by the way, so if you’re right on the borderline of being able to afford that solid-gold Gholdengo, at least you don’t have to worry about paying for a ticket.

title: Japanese airport offering 19,250-yen sandwiches as last Japan meal for international travelers
description: If you want one last taste of Japanese luxury, Kansai International Airport has a restaurant that says it can give it to you in just five minutes. With delicious food being one of the major things that draws travelers to Japan, many people are going to want to splurge on something luxurious for their last […]
content:
If you want one last taste of Japanese luxury, Kansai International Airport has a restaurant that says it can give it to you in just five minutes.

With delicious food being one of the major things that draws travelers to Japan, many people are going to want to splurge on something luxurious for their last meal in the country. On the other hand, with Japan also having tons of non-food-related stuff to see and do, your itinerary might be so full that you don’t have time to slot in anything other than something speedy from the airport before your flight home.

However, if you’re flying out of Japan from Kansai International Airport in Osaka, you can get something quick and decadent…and also very expensive, since Kobist will sell you a fast food sandwich that costs 19,250 yen (US$120).

▼ Kobist

That might sound like an extreme case of airport price-gouging, but this isn’t some ordinary convenience store sandwich (although even those are pretty tasty in Japan). Kobist’s name comes from Kobe, the city with the most exalted beef pedigree in all of Japan, and arguably the world, and the 19,250-yen menu item is their large-size Kobe beef steak sandwich.

Kobist, which opened this past summer, bills itself as a “luxury fast food” restaurant, with the goal of letting travelers enjoy the flavor of authentic Kobe beef even if they only have five minutes to spare. Located inside Terminal 1, in the area past the security check-in for international departures, Kobist is a new venture from Bifteck Kawamura (also known as Bifuteki no Kawamura), a Kobe steak specialist that’s been around since 1972. The chain’s flagship restaurant is in downtown Kobe, but they also have branches in Tokyo’s swanky Ginza and Roppongi districts.

▼ Bifteck Kawamura’s flagship restaurant

So while Kobist is charging 19,250 yen for a sandwich, another way of looking at it is that they’re charging 19,250 yen for a large Kobe steak, which wouldn’t be a record-breaking price, and just serving it with bread wrapped around the meat rather than a dinner roll on the side.

And while Kobist isn’t a budget-priced eatery by any means, it does also have options quite a bit more affordable than its top-of-the-line large Kobe beef steak sandwich. The regular-size version, for example, is about half that price (9,900 yen), and the restaurant also has hamburgers starting at 3,300 yen and steak sandwiches from 3,850 yen made with other types of wagyu/Japanese beef.

Sure, none of those are a highly cost-effective way to fill up before your long flight home, but for meat-loving travelers who don’t know when, or if, they’ll be back in in the country, Kobist would definitely make for a memorable last Japan meal.

description: Pick up a wearable Japanese lesson featuring dinosaurs, hot springs, and deep sea fish. content:
Pick up a wearable Japanese lesson featuring dinosaurs, hot springs, and deep sea fish.

Following the 2011 disaster, Fukushima Prefecture has steadily worked to rebuild its tourism appeal, offering a region filled with natural beauty and history to travelers who seek to venture beyond Japan’s Golden Route of Tokyo, Kyoto, Osaka, and sometimes Hiroshima. In the coastal city of Iwaki, known for its Aquamarine Fukushima aquarium and the tropical Spa Resort Hawaiians, a new attraction at JR Iwaki Station’s S-Pal shopping center offers a fun way to connect with the area, and return with a unique souvenir.

Building on the popularity of the original Fukushima dialect t-shirt vending machine at JR Fukushima Station, this latest Iwaki installment brings the wearable local culture directly to coastal visitors.

▼ The Fukushima Station designs: five for each of the three regions of the prefecture

When people think of Japanese dialects, Kansai-ben from the Kansai region centered around Osaka usually comes to mind. However, Japan features a rich array of regional dialects (hogen, 方言), each reflecting distinct local history and geography. Fukushima itself is divided into three cultural and linguistic zones: Hamadori (the coast, where Iwaki is located), Nakadori (the central valley, home to Fukushima and Koriyama cities), and Aizu (the western mountains, famed for Tsuruga Castle, Kitakata-style ramen, and Higashiyama Hot Spring). Each region boasts its own endearing vocabulary and idioms that sound remarkably different from standard Tokyo Japanese.

These local expressions have become the focus of the Fukushima Dialect T-shirts. Priced at 2,000 yen (US$12.69), each shirt pairs regional phrases with charming illustrations, and the Iwaki vending machine offers a selection of 12 designs that are inspired by local icons and differ from the 15 found in Fukushima’s vending machine.

These coastal Hamadori designs highlight phrases like appatoppa (あっぱとっぱ, “confused” or “flustered”), which features the locally discovered Futabasaurus, and koderanni (こでらんに, “the best” or “can’t get enough of [it]”), depicting Shiramizu Amidado, one of the oldest and most important temples in the Tohoku region.

There are also four designs that showcase beloved Iwaki icons: the mehikari (bigeyed greeneye fish), anko (anglerfish that is used in the traditional hot pot dish anko nabe), hula dance, and Iwaki Yumoto hot spring.

▼ Hula dance helped save the town in the mid-1960s after the local mines closed.

Adding to the excitement, the vending machine operates like a mystery capsule, so after selecting your size of medium, large, or extra large, a random design from the collection is dispensed.

▼ Mehikari are delicious both eaten raw and deep-fried

For both domestic and international visitors, these local dialect mystery T-shirts will serve as warm reminders of your time spent in this region, and be a great conversation starter with Japanese locals wherever you travel. So, whether you are playing to delve into samurai heritage at Tsuraga Castle, walk through the thatched roof village of Ouchijuku, explore the beautiful highlands of Bandai, or enjoy Iwaki’s Pacific coast, consider making a little detour and grabbing one of these T-shirts from the station vending machine, so you can carry it home and wear a slice of Fukushima’s charm.

Starbucks Japan is famous for its exclusive limited-edition goods, and this claim to fame is now set to catapult even further, thanks to a massive new team-up with Pokémon. This new collaboration is one of the biggest we’ve ever seen, with 41 goods adorned in original artwork, and a special Pikachu Honey Cream Latte inviting customers to “Embark on a coffee adventure with Pokémon”.

There’s a lot to get through in this new adventure, so let’s start by taking a look at the star beverage, created from a winning recipe selected from a nationwide Starbucks barista competition that received more than 700 entries. The winning recipe was submitted by Junko Nitta of Starbucks Coffee Koriyama Asaka.

▼ Nitta’s win made her the champion of the Pokémon + Starbucks Barista Battle.

The Pikachu Honey Cream Latte combines espresso with caramel and honey, creating bright yellow hues to mimic Pikachu’s colouring, while the honey-flavoured whipped cream on top is scattered with heart-shaped pieces inspired by the character’s red cheeks. According to Starbucks, the coffee flavours have been gently reined in so the drink can even be enjoyed by people who don’t usually drink coffee.


The drink is available in a Tall size only, priced at 678 yen (US$4.29) to go or 690 yen for dine-in, and every customer who purchases it will receive an original collaboration sticker, while stocks last.

title: Osaka’s amazing budget-luxury hotel has free takoyaki, craft beer, and comedy shows
description: To truly experience the city, OMO7 Osaka is a dream stay for any traveler. When you go traveling in Japan, there are a variety of options from which to choose from, be it hot spring inns or oversized Poké Balls. For our Japanese-language reporter Natsuno Futon, just having a bed and a roof over her […]
content:
To truly experience the city, OMO7 Osaka is a dream stay for any traveler.

When you go traveling in Japan, there are a variety of options from which to choose from, be it hot spring inns or oversized Poké Balls. For our Japanese-language reporter Natsuno Futon, just having a bed and a roof over her head is enough to keep her happy, but several of her friends continued to sing the praises of the OMO brand of hotels run by Hoshino Resorts (operator of unique Japanese hotels like Nara Prison and Tomamu Ice Village), with one friend in particular passionately recommending OMO7 Osaka, and since Natsuno had some plans to visit Osaka, she took this opportunity to try it out.

OMO is based on the concept of an “exciting city center hotel” that is more than simply a place to spend time, but is packed with information and activities to enjoy the city. In fact, Natsuno’s friend has even been on a trip where its entire purpose was to stay at the hotel. The brand has a current total of 18 properties nationwide that are sub-divided into five different categories: OMO1, OMO3, OMO5, OMO7, and Airport, with each type offering different services. The former OMO1 hotels were capsule hotels for minimalistic travelers and provided local guide activities, a neighborhood map, and a comfortable common space for relaxation, but as of September 2026, there are no OMO1 hotels in operation.

The OMO3 basic hotels build on OMO1, although transitioning into individual guest rooms rather than capsules, by also including a grab-and-go breakfast, being good for casual and solo travel, and OMO5 boutique hotels feature a cafe with breakfast options, great for couples:

  • OMO3 Asakusa
  • OMO3 Tokyo Akasaka
  • OMO3 Kyoto Toji
  • OMO5 Otaru
  • OMO5 Hakodate
  • OMO5 Tokyo Otsuka
  • OMO5 Tokyo Gotanda
  • OMO5 Yokohama Bashamichi
  • OMO5 Kanazawa Katamachi
  • OMO5 Kyoto Gion
  • OMO5 Kyoto Sanjo
  • OMO5 Kumamoto
  • OMO5 Okinawa Naha

▼ The sign in front of OMO5 Gotanda in Tokyo

OMO7 is the brand’s full-service hotels, offering extensive in-house facilities, such as breakfast buffets, and a cafe, restaurant, or banquet hall:

  • OMO7 Asahikawa
  • OMO7 Yokohama
  • OMO7 Osaka
  • OMO7 Kochi

Finally, there’s the sole OMO Airport, located right next to Kansai International Airport, with an express buffet, and spa and fitness options.

As Natsuno was looking at the options available to her, she was initially planning on a room-only plan without meals, but there were also family plans with half-price for elementary school students and below, and early bird prices, so it came to about 25,000 yen (US$158.41) for a family of two adults and two children for a single night.

According to Natsuno’s friend, it’s a complete waste if you don’t take advantage of the various activities and enjoy it to the fullest from check-in to check-out, so with that in mind, Natsuno reserved the free guided tour of the nearby Shinsekai area in advance.

The nearest station is Shin-Imamiya Station on the JR and Nankai Railway lines, or the Dobutsuen-mae Station on the Osaka Metro, but this time Natsuno went by JR, and the hotel turned out to be so close that you could see it right from the station platform.

Spreading out in front of the hotel is Miyagurin, a massive green space of about 7,600 square meters (about 1.88 acres) with deck terraces and walking paths surrounding the lawn area, which gives it a sense of openness that makes it hard to believe it’s right next to the station in one of Japan’s biggest cities.

In the common space OMO Base inside the building, there is a gigantic board displaying a map of the surrounding neighborhood.

It introduces spots and shops not often found in guidebooks, gathered by staff who have actually walked around the city, so it serves as a base for exploring the city in a way that you might not have found otherwise.

There are also unique photo items, such as leopard print outfits of the infamous Osaka Obachan aunties, and food samples of kushikatsu (deep-fried skewers).

Also, the quintessential Osaka beverage mixed juice was prepared as a welcome drink. Originating in Shinsekai, the exact same neighborhood as the hotel, classic Osaka mixed juice incorporates milk, crushed ice, and fruits, giving it a thick and rich milkshake-like texture.

Even though the Osakan vibe was embedded throughout, the overall atmosphere didn’t feel cluttered, but rather refined, making for a truly exquisite balance.

Before check-in, it’s possible to leave your luggage in one of the free self-service lockers, decorated by various types of kushikatsu.

There are many wonderful rooms within the hotel, but…

… the room that Natsuno stayed in was the Dandan Room, and she stepped through the door with excitement and nervous anticipation.

Natsuno was greeted with a space resembling a secret base, with beds arranged in two levels, both upper and lower, like a fancy bunk bed.

While certainly looking like a room that kids would instantly fall in love with, Natsuno couldn’t help but admit that she also loved the room a lot.

Despite how large the furniture was, it didn’t feel cramped, and by the window was a spacious sofa that could be unfolded and used as a bed. Natsuno remarked on how stylish it was, and how it was the kind of space that would make you think, “I want to live in a house like this.”

From a parent’s perspective, the fact that the upper bunk is securely enclosed gave Natsuno peace of mind for when her children were sleeping there, and having a large space for luggage was also fantastic.

With a family, the entryway easily gets cluttered with the assortment of shoes being left there, but in this room, the entryway was spacious enough that this wouldn’t become a problem, and having separate bathroom and toilet facilities was a welcome addition.

Plus, the room came stocked with Osaka-style coffee and candies.

Stylish yet easy to use, and on top of that, it brings a sense of excitement. Natsuno soon felt completely comfortable relaxing in her room.

Usually costing an additional 1,000 yen, Natsuno got a glimpse of the public bath area that almost felt like it was an art museum. Even better was that the hotel does not discriminate based on tattoos, allowing tattooed customers use of the bathing facilities, unless the hotel feels the tattoos might cause discomfort to other guests.

However, the true potential of OMO7 Osaka is not limited to just this.

Natsuno had signed up for the free tour exploring Shinsekai, including the Tsutenkaku Tower and Janjan Yokocho, an alley crowded with little eateries and wonders of the past.

The tour was led by a Go-Kinjo (“Neighborhood”) Guide OMO Ranger who knows the area inside out.

The Ranger pointed out details you would miss if you walked by yourselves, recommended shops, and even places that might look a bit intimidating to enter.

Along the way, there was even an experience where you wear clothing typical of an Osaka Obachan to take photos and receive ame-chan (“candies”) at the end. The tour was a wonderfully fun experience and Natsuno highly recommends everyone try it out if they have the time.

There are other activities you can join without reservations, as well as ones that require bookings or have a fee. Natsuno’s friend apparently joined a tour to enjoy kushikatsu and a morning tour themed around dashi (soup stock), which they claimed was “awesome.” Rather than just staying overnight, the hotel creates an opportunity to step out into the town.

At night, Natsuno headed to the guests-only event Osaka Pikapika Night.

When night falls, lantern lights illuminate Miyagurin and Pikapika Yokocho appears, where in addition to delicacies like takoyaki and craft beer, you can also enjoy nostalgic games like target shooting and smart ball, a simpler pinball variant that is also similar to pachinko.

Even for room-only stays, guests elementary school age and above are handed three tickets each, structured so you can choose two items you like from options such as takoyaki, seasonal sweets, or craft beer, and choose one of the games.

To Natsuno, it did not have the atmosphere of a mere cheap service added on as a tacky marketing ploy. The space itself was special: the lawn, the hotel’s giant exterior wall, and the lantern lights all seemed to become one, making it enjoyable just being there.

On top of that, what Natsuno personally loved the most was the main event: Kotekote Show Time.

Comedians from the entertainment company Yoshimoto Kogyo (home to groups like Downtown, Kamaitachi, Chidori, and even All Hanshin Kyojin) and OMO Rangers appear, putting on comedy live shows and a giant bingo utilizing the exterior surface of the hotel wall, which of course hotel guests can enjoy for free as well.

Children and adults alike get excited together, and you can even participate in a simple Osaka-style bon dance. At the end, Natsuno even got a commemorative photo taken with the comedian group Ambitious. It was all too much fun.

Check-out the following day was at 11:00 a.m., so Natsuno spent the morning relaxing, reading books in the facility’s Library Lounge and trying out different stylish chairs to compare them.

Even though she was just relaxing inside the hotel, Natsuno felt like she was spending time a little more mindfully than usual, and experiencing the essence of Osaka at the same time.

In the end, Natsuno stayed right up until the check-out deadline, leaving the hotel while thinking, “I don’t want to go home at all.”

After checking out, soap bubbles and a ring toss game appeared, to which Natsuno really couldn’t say no to having a go at.

On her way out, Natsuno made sure to take a copy of the free booklet that introduces OMO locations nationwide.

Now, Natsuno feels like she can completely understand why her friend stays at one OMO after another. It seems that her friend is now targeting OMO5 Kanazawa Katamachi, but Natsuno has yet to decide where she will end up going, now having become a total fan of OMO.

title: Osaka may name a district after mascot Myaku-Myaku
description: I wonder who will become Myaku-Myaku Mayor. For quite a while now, the ruling political party in Osaka Prefecture, the Japan Innovation Party (Ishin no Kai), has been wanting to change Osaka into a metropolis like Tokyo. This would mainly involve breaking Osaka City into four “special wards,” which are kinds of pseudo-cities with more […]
content:
I wonder who will become Myaku-Myaku Mayor.

For quite a while now, the ruling political party in Osaka Prefecture, the Japan Innovation Party (Ishin no Kai), has been wanting to change Osaka into a metropolis like Tokyo. This would mainly involve breaking Osaka City into four “special wards,” which are kinds of pseudo-cities with more localized governments. 

The benefit would be a reduction in government redundancy, since Osaka Prefecture and Osaka City often oversee similar services and infrastructure in the same areas such as schools, hospitals, and libraries. The downside is it would be a huge pain in the neck to redraw the map and reallocate all of the services, which is probably why the idea was shot down in two referendums over the past decade.

▼ One of the proposed ways to divide Osaka City into four special wards

The Japan Innovation Party remains undeterred, however, and is working hard to keep the dream of an Osaka Metropolis alive. It recently formed a coalition with the nation’s ruling party, the Liberal Democratic Party, with a clear goal of making Osaka Japan’s “Vice Capital,” and what better way to do that than to become more like Tokyo.

Meanwhile, in an effort to bolster more public support for the metropolis idea, the Japan Innovation Party held an online survey where citizens of Osaka would vote for what they would like the new special wards to be named. Among the more lackluster choices named after geographic locations or directions, some citizen suggested “Myakumya Ward” as a possible name for the area along the north side of the current Osaka City.

The reason for this choice is that the Japanese word for “Ward” is “Ku,” so Myakumya Ward in Japanese would be “Myakumya-ku,” nearly identical to the popular mascot of the Osaka Expo, Myaku-Myaku.

▼ Yes, all over the country there have been outbreaks of Myaku-Myaku fever.

Government officials involved in the survey weren’t sure what to do with the proposed name. On one hand, it seems to make a mockery of the whole idea. On the other hand, people love a good mockery, and since the whole purpose of this survey is to generate interest in the project, Myakumya Ward is very likely the best way to accomplish that.

The full shortlist of names is the following:

  1. Osaka Yodogawa Ward, Osaka Kita Ward, Osaka Chuo Ward, Osaka Tennoji Ward
  2. Shin-Osaka Ward, Umeda Ward, Namba Ward, Tennoji Ward
  3. Yumeshima Ward, Shirokita Ward, Semba Ward, Uemachi Ward
  4. Myakumya Ward, Kita Ward, Minami Ward, Harukas Ward

The second set seems like the most sensible. Most people I talk to refer to those general areas by those major train station names anyway. “Shin-Osaka” not so much, though, and looking at the options, I kind of think “Myakumya” is the best choice for that area, which contains the site of the former Expo. I would have said “Yodogawa,” but they put that meaningless “Osaka” in front of it for some reason, so “Myakumya” it is!

Reaction to the name online was mixed but significantly leaning towards the opinion that naming a municipal district after a gooey creature is a bad idea.

“It would be embarrassing to have to write ‘Myakumyaku’ on official documents.”
“Eh, I don’t live there, so I say go for it!”
“I think if they really own it wholeheartedly, it could become a good thing.”
“I think Governor Yoshimura said flat out on a livestream that it’ll never happen.”
“I like Myakumya-ku, it sounds like a land of magical monsters.”
“We can’t do that. We’d be the laughing stock of future generations.”
“They should call it Neo-Kobe.”
“The people who have to live there should have the biggest say in that.”
“Say goodbye to property values there.”
“I can’t wait to hand out business cards that say I’m from Myakumya-ku.”
“I’m expecting Fah Ward to come up soon too.”
“I live here, and I really hate this idea.”

Ultimately, we probably should respect the wishes of people who live in Myaku-Myaku Land, because they deserve to live with dignity too. Quite frankly though, Shin-Osaka (literally “New Osaka”) sounds like some kind of sci-fi Evangelion setting, and it would just be plain wrong since it’ll literally have become old Osaka at that point. Yumeshima is also the site of an upcoming integrated resort and casino, so do people really want their special ward to be named after that?

I think the people there just need to marinate on the idea a bit, and they’ll come to realize that Myakumya Ward really is the only sensible choice here.

title: Do Japan’s new single-minded convenience store bento show depressing poverty or satisfying focus?
description: The line between simplicity and inadequacy can be a fine one. Which side do Lawson’s new Ittentoppasugi fall on? 9 times out of 10, there’s an excited spring in our step as we walk through the door of our local Japanese convenience store on the release day for a new bento boxed lunch. As we […]
content:
The line between simplicity and inadequacy can be a fine one. Which side do Lawson’s new Ittentoppasugi fall on?

9 times out of 10, there’s an excited spring in our step as we walk through the door of our local Japanese convenience store on the release day for a new bento boxed lunch. As we crossed over the threshold into Lawson on September 22, though, our emotional state was more complicated.

Lawson is calling its newest bento series Ittentoppasugi, which basically translates to “super single-minded.” That’s a bit of a warning sign already, since a big part of the appeal of bento is that you usually get a number of different side dishes to go along with the rice that they always contain. Any pretense of variety is swept away for the Ittentoppasugi bento, which consist of rice, one topping ingredient, and absolutely nothing else.

In other words, in any individual Ittentoppasugi bento you’re only getting as much variety as you would in a rice ball with a single type of filling. Actually, even rice balls usually have a longer list of ingredients, since a lot of them come wrapped in seaweed. Because of that, a lot of the online reactions when Lawson first announced the Ittentoppasugi series wasn’t so much joy at its focus, but sadness that this is another sign of how rising prices in Japan seem to be affecting every aspect of daily life, eroding even such simple pleasures as affordable convenience store food.

With prices for conventional boxed lunches continuing to climb, the 297-yen (US$1.90) starting price for Lawson’s single-minded bento are, however, an intriguing offer for those who’ve given up on buying more expensive alternatives. So we were willing to give the new boxed lunches a try, and procured an Ittentoppasugi salmon bento and an Ittentoppasugi sausage bento for taste-testing purposes.

As you can see, there’s nothing inside the salmon bento but rice, salmon flakes, and an almost palpable sense of poverty. You do at least get quite a lot of rice, though. The total weight of the single-minded salmon bento is approximately 260 grams (9.2 ounces). We didn’t weigh the packaging or minuscule amount of salmon, but even collectively they can’t weight all that much, meaning there’s a lot more than the 160 grams of rice that’s considered the standard serving size in Japan.

And while there’s not a lot of salmon, our expectations were raised by it being bodakko. Bodakko is a kind of heavily salted salmon that’s popular in Akita Prefecture, a part of Japan that’s famous for its high-quality rice. Because it’s so salty, even a small amount of bodakko is said to make a large quantity of rice taste extra-delicious, and bento with a high rice-to-salmon ratio are kind of a regional specialty of Akita.

Taking a taste, we learned that the Ittentoppasugi bodakko bento’s salmon is considerably saltier than the flaked salmon found in most bento or rice balls, but not shockingly so. As a matter of fact, we don’t think it would overpower our taste buds even without any rice to take alternating bites of.

It’s perfectly tasty salmon, though we still could have done with a greater quantity of fish. Eating at a natural pace, we had about one-fourth of the bento’s rice left when we’d finished off the last flake of salmon, which we then had to consume by itself.

Next it was time to try the Ittentoppasugi sausage bento.

This is a premium-priced Ittentoppasugi bento, but even that means that it’s still just 397 yen. It’s also heftier than its cheaper bodakko brethren, weighing in at just over 300 grams.

The sausage Ittentoppasugi also has a stronger foundation to stand on as to Lawson’s claim that single-mindedness is its reason for existence. Sure, you still get only one non-rice element, sliced sausage, but you get a lot of it, and there’s a sort of decadence to be found in such a large quality of inexpensive meat, making this feel like a cheap indulgence more than no-other-option poverty chow.

They even spruce up the sausage a bit, dressing it with a light teriyaki-style sauce that imparts some additional savory sweetness.

There’s no way to convince your brain that either of these bento are luxury dining, but they both accomplish what they set out to do. They’re two of the most affordable and easily accessible bento boxed lunches in all of Japan, and though the ingredient list is short, everything inside those boxes tastes good, and after having tried these two Ittentoppasugi, we might have to consider trying Lawson’s upcoming single-minded corn bento too.

title: 7-Eleven Japan revamps its convenience store pizza, but did it ruin a good thing?
description: We find out if 7-Eleven delivers on its promise to enhance the size and texture of its pizzas. 7-Elevens in Japan are a cut above those in other places of the world, with hot food so good you’d hardly believe it was from a convenience store. One of the chain’s most popular hot food options […]
content:
We find out if 7-Eleven delivers on its promise to enhance the size and texture of its pizzas.

7-Elevens in Japan are a cut above those in other places of the world, with hot food so good you’d hardly believe it was from a convenience store. One of the chain’s most popular hot food options is its pizza, baked in dedicated in-store ovens to give it a freshly made texture and flavour.

However, for some reason, 7-Eleven recently decided the pizzas were due for a revamp, announcing that they would be enhancing the chewiness and increasing the size by approximately 30 percent, without changing the price.

The change went into effect on 15 September, so we immediately ordered the new pizza for delivery – yes, 7-Eleven delivers pizzas through the chain’s official 7NOW delivery app – choosing the Margherita (780 yen [US$4.94]) out of the two options, with the other option being Teriyaki Chicken, for 880 yen.

▼  The first thing to surprise us was the box itself, which had changed from a slightly octagonal shape…

▼ …to a plain square one.

If this was one way for the company to cut corners in an effort to revamp the pizza without changing the price, then we had no complaints. The box still looked great, and when we lifted the lid, we found a pizza inside that measured around 23 centimetres (9 inches) across.

Having reviewed the pizza a while back, before the change, this was roughly 3 centimetres bigger than before, amounting to an increase in diameter of around 15 percent, which, when doing the math, equates to an increased surface area of around 30 percent.

▼ Having confirmed that the size increase was no exaggeration, it was now time to give the pizza a taste.

Taking a bite, the flavours of cheese and tomato gently spread through the palate, accompanied by a satisfying chewiness. The flavour and texture were excellent, and we noticed that our teeth seemed to sink further into the dough than before.

According to the chain, a special method has been used to increase the moisture content of the dough, and as you work your way through each slice, the added chewiness becomes more evident, and more addictive, thanks to the extra hydration.

▼ The moisture content comes at no expense to the base, either, as it still has a good thickness.

▼ The crust is nice and chewy too.

Being able to improve the size and texture of the pizza while maintaining the price, flavour and thickness is no easy task, yet 7-Eleven manages to pull it off impressively. When we reviewed the previous pizza, we described it as occupying a position somewhere between a frozen pizza and one from a specialist pizza restaurant, and that position is now even more firmly established in our minds.

In fact, the pizza may now be occupying special territory as a brand in its own right, with a signature flavour, texture and price that reflects 7-Eleven’s commitment to delivering satisfaction for its customers. Like the chain’s highly acclaimed smoothies, the pizzas really are worth stopping by for.

title: Lady Gaga and Family Mart team up for a Japanese convenience store work video [Video]
description: Can the recording star make people gaga over the idea of working at Family Mart? Family Mart has been making a big push to establish itself as the fashionable choice within the Japanese convenience store space. Sometimes in the literal sense of having its own apparel line, and sometimes in the sense of cultivating a […]
content:
Can the recording star make people gaga over the idea of working at Family Mart?

Family Mart has been making a big push to establish itself as the fashionable choice within the Japanese convenience store space. Sometimes in the literal sense of having its own apparel line, and sometimes in the sense of cultivating a fresh, avant garde approach to store design, even if that means making some of its convenience stores feel a little less convenient.

Family Mart’s latest stylish strategy? Recruiting none other than international pop star Lady Gaga to promote the chain.

Set to the sounds of her song “Killah,” the video shows Gaga dance-working a shift at Family Mart. The visuals are in black and white except for the green and blue of the Family Mart signage, helping the colors really pop and establishing an atmospheric sci-fi flare. Adding to that vibe is Gaga’s outfit, a futuristic reimagining of Family Mart’s themselves-new employee uniforms which were just introduced to the chain at the start of this month.

Yes, as indicated by the “Family Mart Staff” written on her top, the video casts Gaga as part of the convenience store’s crew, since while her star power is drawing attention to the chain in general, it’s specifically meant as a recruitment promotion to drum up excitement for the idea of working at Family Mart, which is why the video ends with her asking “Famima de hataraku?,” or “Do you want to work at Family Mart?”

Gaga doesn’t appear to have been in Japan since this past January, and the recruitment commercial was actually filmed in Los Angeles at a studio-built Family Mart replica. In an interview conducted after filming, though, Gaga mentioned that she has visited Family Marts while in Japan, and that while she loves traditional Japanese fare such as sushi and cold soba, she’s also very fond of Family Mart’s cooked-in-store Famichiki boneless fried chicken.

▼ Really, everybody loves Famichiki.

So will this video, set to air as a commercial on Japanese TV and play inside Family Mart stores, lead to a flood of applications from people swayed by Gaga’s dance moves to apply for jobs at Family Mart? It’s hard to say. Obviously, there’s zero chance of the chart-topping recording artist herself giving up her current lifestyle to stock shelves with the new Family Mart seasonal sweet potato sweets or make sure that the branch’s Monster Wolf is in proper operating order. Japanese audiences tend to take a less literal, arguably rosier-tinted interpretation of celebrity endorsement, however, and famous Japanese entertainment industry stars lending their auras to more plebeian projects, including job-hunting services, has been a part of the media landscape here for a while, so the implied thumbs-up towards convenience store work will probably have some extent of positive effect on Family Mart’s brand image, and by extension its recruiting efforts.
